title: Day 5 of letting an AI trading agent run a small real account: two more boring names, placed overnight, and I still didn't save its reasons
author: Accomplished_Fun_408
selftext:
Disclosure: I work at Flow AI, the company behind Bobby AI, an AI trading agent, and RockFlow, the brokerage the account sits at. My own money, small size, under $2K at risk. Not advice, my own calls.

Days 1 to 17 come from the broker's order export and I'm posting them this week; it goes live after that. Day 1 is in my post history.

Day 3, Sept 23. Before the open it proposed a second share of AMZN. Order placed at 03:23 ET with a $255.45 limit, filled pre-market at 07:37 at $255.45, fee $1.40. Same name twice in three days. I asked nothing and confirmed.

Day 4 into Day 5, Sept 24 to 25. In the evening it proposed two more: three NVDA with a $223.82 limit and six KO at $88.20. Both placed overnight. KO filled pre-market at 04:00 ET at $88.20, NVDA at 10:15 at $223.82. Fees $1.40 and $1.41.

Where the account stands on Day 5: AMZN two shares, $511. NVDA three, $671. KO six, $529. $1,712 in three names, nothing sold. SPY closed at $771.35 on Sept 25, down 0.3% from Day 1.

What I notice: it buys with small limit orders placed outside market hours, all four fills were limits, two of them overnight. It has not proposed a sell, or a size above six shares, or anything I would describe as exciting. Six shares of Coca-Cola from an AI trading agent. I buy 0DTE calls, as you'll see on Day 15. The contrast is the experiment.

What I still didn't do: save its reasons. A commenter on Day 1 said confirm-every-order decays into a rubber stamp by day 30. By Day 5 I was already there. From the live part of the log, every order gets four things: its reason, the one condition that would make the trade wrong, my one-line reply to that, and two timestamps, proposed and confirmed. Each week I'll report how many I cleared in under ten seconds.

Question: when your agent proposes the same name twice in three days with no new information, do you confirm the second one, or make it argue?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: I would make it argue, but against its own prior thesis rather than from scratch. On the second AMZN proposal within three days, show the first rationale and invalidation condition, then require the agent to identify what changed and whether it is adding exposure or expressing a genuinely new view. Since the original reasons were not saved, the two proposed/confirmed timestamps and your under-ten-second approvals cannot reveal whether you evaluated anything. I would also predefine a rule for repeated names, otherwise confirmation speed may measure habituation more than oversight.

replies.author: robbyedit
replies.body: You need a memory system otherwise the LLM will have no idea of what it has done in the past

replies.author: Accomplished_Fun_408
replies.body: It does keep memory across sessions, it knows what I've declined and how I like to size. What I haven't tested is whether it brings its own earlier rationale back on its own when it repeats a name. That's the next repeat's test: before I confirm, I'll ask it what it said last time and see if it can answer without me pasting it in. The log I'm keeping is for me, not for it.

replies.author: Accomplished_Fun_408
replies.body: Making it argue against its own prior thesis is the version I'll use: on a repeat name it has to show me the earlier rationale and invalidation first, then say what changed and whether this is adding exposure or a new view. And you're right about Days 1 to 17, with no saved reasons the timestamps measure habituation, not oversight. That's why the live rules start with the log. One rule I haven't settled: the window. Same name within five sessions? And does a declared averaging plan, three buys spread over a month, get to skip the argument, or does each leg still have to justify itself?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I'd make it argue, and the cheapest way is a rule: a repeat proposal for the same name within a few days needs a stated new reason (new information, price level or position gap), otherwise it's flagged as a duplicate. Logging how long you take to confirm is a good idea, since the median time and the share cleared in under ten seconds show when review has turned into a rubber stamp. Limit orders placed overnight also deserve a check on fill quality against the open, because pre-market fills are often thinner. Overnight proposals around earnings or CPI days are where context matters most, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source for flagging them.
